nodes.front: Example 1 · Connect representations: Why was each side of the equation written with an equivalent expression using 2 as the base?
nodes.back: Listen for: In order to solve an exponential equation, the bases must be the same.

nodes.front: Example 1 · Connect representations: Could the expressions have been rewritten by using a common base of (1/2), 4, or 10 rather than 2?
nodes.back: Listen for: The expressions could be rewritten with a common base of (1/2) or 4. They could also be rewritten with a common base of 10, however, this would make the equation more complex rather than drawing closer to a solution.

nodes.front: Example 5 · Connect representations: What is an extraneous solution and how do they occur?
nodes.back: Listen for: An extraneous solution is a root of a transformed equation that is not a root of the original equation. They occur when you transform an equation in order to solve it, without regard to the domain of the original equation.

nodes.front: Example 5 · Check student thinking: Why is (-5) an extraneous solution (part a), but (-1/2) is not extraneous (part b)?
nodes.back: Listen for: In part b, a negative x-value results in a positive argument for the natural log. But in part a, a negative x-value results in a negative argument for the logarithm with base 5, resulting in an expression that is undefined.

A biologist uses n = k log(A) for the number of a species n on a land mass of area A. a. Use the graph (points (100, 1000) and (1000, 1500)) to determine k. b. Determine the land mass in acres needed to support 3,000 of the species.

a. 500 (1000 = k log 100 = 2k; check 500 log 1000 = 1500). b. 1,000,000 acres (3000 = 500 log A, log A = 6, A = 10^6). Tied to kept Example 5 by the TE item analysis (43 and 46 are the lesson's only DOK 3 items); students must choose a point, solve for k, then undo the log, which no IXL skill asks. …
A store sells two fitness trackers until TrackSmart sales exceed FitTracker sales. Weekly sales, weeks 1-4: FitTracker 28, 54, 112, 228; TrackSmart 5, 17, 44, 130.

A. Model With Mathematics: find an equation of an exponential function that models the sales for each fitness tracker. Describe your method. (TE: regression, y = 13.6266(2.0180)^x and y = 1.8081(2.9227)^x)
B. Based on the equations that you wrote, determine when the store will stop selling FitTracker. (TE: the graphs intersect near x = 6, so after 6 weeks)

Why do you think an exponential model is better than a linear or a quadratic model for this problem? → Sales are not increasing at a constant rate, so a linear model would not make sense; nothing in the data suggests a downward turn, so a quadratic model would not make sense.
How do you know that TrackSmart will outsell FitTracker at some point? → TrackSmart is increasing at a greater rate, so eventually its sales will be greater.
How can you use the equations to determine when the store will stop selling FitTracker? → Evaluate each model for different numbers of weeks until FitTracker sales are less than TrackSmart sales.
Graph the two equations you found. Does your graph verify your results? Explain. → Yes; the x-coordinate of the intersection is when TrackSmart begins to exceed FitTracker.
Why did different methods result in the same answer for Part B? → The methods differ, but the equations themselves should be fairly alike.
